vignette:
Marcus

Marcus is twenty-one years old, recently married, and has not worked in nearly eight months. He does not describe himself as unemployed so much as someone who simply stopped being able to leave the house with any regularity. The distinction matters to him, though he struggles to explain exactly why.

The event that changed everything happened on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon last spring. Marcus and his younger brother Luka, who was seventeen at the time, were riding home together on their motorbikes along a rural road they had taken hundreds of times. A car drifted across the centre line. Marcus, riding slightly ahead, heard the impact before he saw it. He remembers the sound — a flat, dense collision that did not sound like anything he had words for — and then turning around to find Luka on the ground, the car already stopped fifty metres up the road. He ran to his brother and knelt beside him on the asphalt. He held Luka's hand and talked to him until the ambulance arrived. He has never described to anyone exactly what he saw in those minutes, only that he was certain, completely certain, that his brother was dying.

Luka survived. He spent three weeks in hospital with a fractured pelvis, a broken collarbone, and a serious head injury. He is alive and recovering, living now with their parents. By most measures, the story has a good ending. Marcus knows this. He repeats it to himself often, and the repetition does nothing to help.

In the weeks after the accident, Marcus found he could not sleep for more than two or three hours at a stretch. When he did sleep, he returned to the road. He woke from these dreams drenched in sweat, his heart hammering, sometimes already on his feet before he was fully conscious. His wife, Elena, learned quickly not to touch him when he woke that way. He had grabbed her wrist once without meaning to, and the shame of that moment sits with him still.

He has not ridden a motorbike since the accident. He sold his within the month. He avoids the road where it happened by a wide margin, adding twenty minutes to any journey that would otherwise take him near it. He gave up his job at a local warehouse partly because the route to work passed too close, and partly because he found he could no longer concentrate well enough to operate the machinery safely. He is aware that this explanation is only partly true. The fuller truth is that he could not face being around people who might ask how Luka was doing, because answering that question required him to go back to the road.

At home, Marcus is watchful in a way that exhausts him. He checks the locks before bed and then checks them again. He sits with his back to walls in restaurants and rarely agrees to go to restaurants at all. He startles badly at sudden sounds — a door slamming, a car backfiring — and afterwards feels a hot flush of embarrassment that he cannot quite suppress. Elena has noticed that he has become quieter, more withdrawn, quicker to irritability. He knows she has noticed. He does not know how to explain to her that the irritability is not directed at her, that it comes from somewhere he cannot locate or name, a constant low-grade tension that never fully releases.

What troubles Marcus most, in the quiet moments he cannot avoid, is the feeling that something fundamental shifted on that road. He had always understood himself as someone capable and present, the older brother who looked out for others. Now he finds himself moving through his days with a sense of unreality, as though he is watching his own life from a slight distance. He loves Elena. He is grateful Luka is alive. He holds both of these things and finds that they are not enough to bring him back to himself. He is still on the road, kneeling on the asphalt, waiting to find out what happens next.
